input_signals.name: Capex Surge Against Cash-Flow Debt Service
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm spending far above its own recent capital-budget norm is only penalized when its operating cash flow is too thin to service existing liabilities; that combination signals an escalation that must be funded externally under stress, whereas a distressed firm spending below its own norm is credibly retrenching to preserve solvency.
input_signals.reasoning: The investment leg is a firm-relative capex surge (capex versus its own three-year average), not total asset growth, so it is orthogonal to the Cooper-Gulen-Schill construct and to CMA; the distress leg is the Beaver/Ohlson cash-flow-to-liabilities ratio rather than a leverage tilt. Centering the investment term with ZSCORE and weighting it by a distress rank in [0,1] makes the signal near-zero for financially sound firms, so the spread is a genuine interaction with an interpretable long leg (distressed retrenchers) rather than an amplified investment main effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ratio( capx, ma( capx, 3 ) ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( ratio( oancf, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capex Financed at Short Maturity
input_signals.hypothesis: Long-lived capital investment funded against a heavy stock of debt maturing within a year creates a maturity mismatch: the asset pays off over a decade while the liability must be rolled next quarter, so these firms bear rollover risk that is punished when credit conditions tighten.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a distinct fragility channel from leverage level or liquidity buffer — a firm can be modestly levered and still be dangerously short-funded — and it interacts naturally with the duration of the investment being made. The distress leg scales current debt by current assets, the pool actually available to retire it, so the signal isolates mismatch rather than size or leverage.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( capx, ppent ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, act ) ) )

input_signals.name: Headcount Expansion Without Debt Service Capacity
input_signals.hypothesis: Adding employees is a quasi-fixed commitment that is far harder to reverse than capex; when a firm expands headcount while earnings are too small relative to its liability stock, it is locking in an operating cost base it cannot fund, and subsequent layoffs and restructuring charges are underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: This moves the investment leg off the balance sheet entirely and onto the real side, so it cannot be a rescaling of asset growth, capex intensity, or any accrual-based construct already in the archive. Because labor commitments carry no collateral value, the distress interaction should be sharper for employment growth than for capital growth — a directly testable contrast against the capex-based signals in this batch.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( emp, 1 ) ), rank( neg( ratio( ib, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Levered Firms Sweating Installed Capacity
input_signals.hypothesis: Among highly levered firms, rising sales per unit of installed property and equipment shows management generating growth from assets already owned rather than from new commitments; this capital-efficient resilience is undervalued, while levered firms whose capacity utilization is falling are heading toward covenant trouble.
input_signals.reasoning: The gen-0 positive-sign attempt failed (alpha -1.7% against a positive prediction) because balance-sheet rotation into cash is itself a distress symptom rather than a discipline signal; utilization improvement is a genuine operating-performance channel that separates resilient levered firms from shrinking ones. Centering the utilization change and weighting by the leverage rank means unlevered firms contribute near zero, so both legs are populated by levered firms and the spread is an interaction rather than a leverage tilt.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( rank( delta( ratio( sale, ppent ), 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft-Asset Expansion Without Earnings Cushion
input_signals.hypothesis: Expansion that adds intangible and goodwill-type assets rather than tangible capacity produces collateral that lenders will not accept and that must be impaired if performance disappoints; when the acquiring firm's pretax income is small relative to its liabilities, such soft-asset growth signals overpayment and imminent write-downs rather than franchise building.
input_signals.reasoning: The asset-quality composition of investment is a channel untouched by the archive, which has so far tested capex, inventory, headcount, and total-asset growth — all of which are collateralizable in a way intangibles are not, so the distress interaction should be sharply stronger here. Pretax income scaled by liabilities captures the debt-service cushion that determines whether an impairment triggers covenant trouble, giving a clean conditional reading rather than a repackaged profitability tilt.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( delta( intan, 1 ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( pi, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Escalating Capex Into Deteriorating Profitability
input_signals.hypothesis: Distress is a trajectory, not a level: a firm whose return on assets has been sliding for several years and which nevertheless raises capital spending is escalating commitment to a failing business, while a firm on the same downward trajectory that cuts spending is adapting, and the market prices the two alike.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing a static distress ratio with the multi-year slope of profitability makes the conditioning variable a state transition rather than an Altman-style level, so the signal cannot load on the RMW-like main effect that static profitability proxies carry. Centering the capex-growth leg while keeping the deterioration weight in [0,1] means healthy or improving firms contribute near zero, so both extremes of the sort are populated by deteriorating firms and the spread isolates the escalation-versus-adaptation contrast.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( rank( growth( capx, 1 ) ) ), rank( neg( trend( ratio( ib, at ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Inventory Growth Financed by Deteriorating Current Position
input_signals.hypothesis: Stock building is most dangerous when it is being financed by stretching payables and other current obligations, so that the current position is visibly deteriorating in the same year the inventory is added; the firm is converting near-term liquidity into unsold goods.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's best-alpha inventory signal conditioned on the *level* of working capital, which the critic correctly noted is mechanically linked to inventory itself; conditioning instead on the *year-over-year deterioration in the current ratio* breaks that mechanical overlap and identifies the financing source of the buildup rather than its accounting footprint. This isolates static-versus-dynamic distress conditioning within the family that has worked best.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( invt, 1 ) ), rank( delta( ratio( lct, act ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity Growth While Claims Outrun Revenue
input_signals.hypothesis: Solvency is a race between the growth of obligations and the growth of the revenue that must service them; a firm expanding gross plant while its liabilities compound faster than its sales is building capacity on a claim structure the business is not growing into.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the MIN experiment with a growth-rate mismatch makes the distress leg a dynamic solvency concept — the wedge between liability growth and revenue growth — rather than another level ratio drawn from the same balance-sheet dimensions already tested. It also avoids the correlation problem the critic identified, since the conditioner is a difference of growth rates and is close to orthogonal to the level of leverage, liquidity, or profitability.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), rank( sub( growth( lt, 1 ), growth( sale, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Scale Instability Without Debt Service Capacity
input_signals.hypothesis: The archive shows that fragile firms are punished both when they expand and when they contract, which means the operative variable is not the direction of adjustment but its magnitude: a firm with insufficient earnings to cover its liabilities that is violently resizing its labor force and capital base in either direction is adjusting under duress, while a fragile firm holding scale steady is managing its constraints.
input_signals.reasoning: This resolves rather than repeats the sign contradiction the critic identified — Headcount Expansion (fmb -2.54) and Fire-Sale Disinvestment (alpha -3.5%) used the same NEG(ib/lt) conditioner with opposite investment signs and both worked, which is only coherent if the relation is U-shaped in adjustment magnitude. Taking absolute growth in both factor inputs and ranking their sum tests that U-shape directly, a hypothesis no archived signal can express.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sumrank( abs( growth( emp, 1 ) ), abs( growth( ppent, 1 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( ib, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Inventory Buildup Against A Maturity Wall
input_signals.hypothesis: Converting cash into unsold goods is most dangerous when a large share of the firm's debt matures within the year: the working capital is locked in exactly when the claims come due, forcing either a distressed inventory liquidation or a refinancing on unfavourable terms.
input_signals.reasoning: This crosses the archive's two most productive legs from opposite families — inventory growth carries a correctly signed slope and a -3.1% alpha with a raw Sharpe of -0.35, while the short-maturity share produced the strongest alpha t-statistic in the archive (-4.72) — so the pairing is the most direct route to joint slope-and-alpha evidence rather than one or the other. Neither leg is a rescaling of the other and both are high-coverage annual balance-sheet items.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( invt, 1 ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Equity Raised Beyond Investment Needs
input_signals.hypothesis: Equity sold in excess of the year's capital spending is not funding projects — it is funding the retirement of claims or the replacement of lost working capital; when the firm simultaneously faces a large share of debt maturing within the year, the issuance is a creditor-driven rescue rather than an owner-driven investment decision.
input_signals.reasoning: Netting capital expenditure out of the issuance measure directly addresses the critique that raw sstk/at is the published share-issuance anomaly: a growth firm raising equity to fund a large capital program now scores near zero, while a firm raising equity it does not invest scores high, which is precisely the rescue-financing construct the hypothesis describes. The maturity-wall conditioner then separates rescue issuance from opportunistic issuance, making the interaction the identifying element rather than a tilt on a known main effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( sstk, capx ), at ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Inventory Overhang State At The Maturity Wall
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters for a firm facing near-term maturities is not how fast inventory grew last year but whether the stock of goods is unusually large relative to the revenue it must generate; a firm sitting at the top of its own five-year inventory-to-sales range has an overhang that will only clear through discounting.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates a specific design choice on the archive's best joint signal — a persistent state versus a one-year flow — which matters because the flow version may work only through the accrual and asset-growth components it shares with published effects, whereas the state version is scaled by revenue and cannot be. If the state version retains the alpha and the slope, the mechanism is genuinely about stock overhang meeting rollover risk rather than about growth accounting.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ts_rank( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Receivables Lock-Up At The Maturity Wall
input_signals.hypothesis: If the mechanism behind the archive's best joint signal is genuinely about liquidity being locked into unconvertible assets, it should operate through receivables as well as goods: a firm that has extended far more credit to customers while a large share of its own debt matures within the year has financed its buyers instead of its lenders.
input_signals.reasoning: Subtracting inventory as well as cash removes the double-count the critic identified and leaves a receivables-and-other-current-asset channel that is genuinely disjoint from the parent signal's leg, making this a discrimination test rather than a re-pairing. If it works, the mechanism is general working-capital lock-up meeting rollover risk; if only the inventory version works, the effect is about unsold product specifically, and either answer directs the final generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( sub( sub( act, che ), invt ), 1 ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Dual Lock-Up Overhang At The Maturity Wall
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), sale), 5))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Liquidity can be locked up in goods or in customer credit, and a firm sitting at the top of its own five-year range on both — with a large share of debt maturing within the year — has committed its entire operating liquidity to assets it cannot convert before the claims fall due.
input_signals.reasoning: The two channels have now been tested separately against the same conditioner and both produced slopes near -3.5 with negative alphas, and because receivables are measured here net of inventory the two ranked states are genuinely disjoint rather than double-counted. Scaling each by sales and ranking within firm history preserves the state construction that beat the growth-rate version, so this should compound the two effects rather than dilute either.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sumrank( ts_rank( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ), ts_rank( ratio( sub( sub( act, che ), invt ), sale ), 5 ) ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Overhang Against Pure Maturity Structure
input_signals.hypothesis: What creates rollover pressure is the share of *borrowing* that must be repaid within the year, not the share of total liabilities: a firm whose debt is overwhelmingly short-dated faces a refinancing decision every twelve months, and if its inventory is simultaneously at an historic high relative to sales it will meet that decision without liquid resources.
input_signals.reasoning: The conditioner behind every large alpha in this archive is dlc/lt, whose denominator includes payables, accruals and deferred items, so the critic's standing concern that it partly proxies for total leverage has never been tested; replacing the denominator with total interest-bearing debt isolates maturity structure from leverage magnitude. If the alpha and slope survive, the mechanism is confirmed as refinancing timing rather than a leverage tilt, which is the single most valuable robustness result available before the final generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ts_rank( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, add( dlc, dltt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Liquid Reserve Shifting Into Goods At The Maturity Wall
input_signals.hypothesis: Within a firm's convertible resources, the split between cash and unsold goods determines whether a maturity can be met; a firm whose cash share of that pool has fallen sharply has rotated repayment capacity into product just as its debt comes due.
input_signals.reasoning: Expressing the rotation as the change in a bounded share — cash divided by cash plus inventory, which lies in the unit interval — removes the unbounded cash-growth term the critic identified as noise-dominating while measuring exactly the same reallocation decision. Because it is a composition change rather than a level or a growth rate, it is also cleanly distinct from both the archived inventory-growth and inventory-overhang legs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, add( che, invt ) ), 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Inventory Overhang Against Quick-Asset Coverage
input_signals.hypothesis: Rollover pressure is properly measured as debt due divided by the assets that can actually pay it — cash and receivables — rather than as a share of total liabilities; a firm whose maturing debt exceeds its quick assets and whose inventory is at an historic high has no route to repayment other than refinancing.
input_signals.reasoning: Two conditioner reformulations were tested last generation and both were informative but weaker than dlc/lt, which suggests the missing ingredient is not maturity structure or cash alone but the ratio of what is due to what is convertible; this construction embeds the quick-asset insight that produced the archive's largest alpha directly into the conditioner. It also avoids the near-zero denominator instability of che/dlc, since quick assets are strictly positive for essentially all firms.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ts_rank( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, sub( act, invt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Dual Overhang Against Quick-Asset Coverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), sale), 5))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, SUB(act, invt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The firms that underperform are those whose operating liquidity is simultaneously consumed on both working-capital channels and whose maturing debt is large relative to the quick assets left over; both conditions are needed, and each is measured on the dimension that matters.
input_signals.reasoning: This pairs the investment leg with the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope against the coverage-based conditioner motivated in S2, so it is the leanest combination of the two best-validated components rather than a stack of everything. Running it alongside S1 and S2 also decomposes cleanly: if S5 beats both parents, the improvement comes from the conditioner; if S1 beats S5, it comes from adding the structural quick-asset level.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sumrank( ts_rank( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ), ts_rank( ratio( sub( sub( act, che ), invt ), sale ), 5 ) ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, sub( act, invt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Releasing Working Capital While Terming Out Debt
input_signals.hypothesis: The resilience case is a firm actively converting its balance sheet back into cash and using that flexibility to push its debt out: destocking relative to sales frees liquidity, and a falling short-debt share shows creditors accepting longer terms, together describing a firm repairing itself before it is forced to.
input_signals.reasoning: The one long-side mechanism that has produced alpha in this archive is creditor-granted maturity extension (+3.6%, t=+3.04), and pairing it with working-capital release rather than with capital spending removes the investment-anomaly headwind that the critic identified as the weakness of the capex-based version. It is the precise economic mirror of the flagship short signal, so a positive result would confirm the interaction is continuous across the whole distribution rather than a tail phenomenon.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( delta( ratio( invt, sale ), 1 ) ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( dlc, lt ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Weeks-Of-Sales Overhang Weighted By Rollover Risk
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The damage from an inventory overhang scales with its size in weeks of sales, not with where it ranks in the cross-section, and that magnitude should be amplified in proportion to how much debt is coming due — a firm two months of sales above its norm facing a maturity wall is in a materially different position from one a day above it.
input_signals.reasoning: The previous version collapsed the cardinal deviation back to an ordering with an outer RANK, so this leaves the deviation in its natural units — winsorized at the one-percent tails for robustness — and lets the magnitude enter the product directly against the bounded conditioner rank. That makes the signal genuinely magnitude-weighted rather than rank-weighted, which is the design question the flagship mechanism still has open.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( sub( ratio( invt, sale ), ma( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ), 1 ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cardinal Dual Overhang At The Maturity Wall
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(ADD(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), SUB(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), sale), MA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), sale), 5))), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Total operating liquidity consumed is the sum of the excess weeks of sales tied up in goods and the excess weeks tied up in customer credit, both measured against the firm's own normal operating level; that combined excess, amplified by the share of debt falling due within the year, is what leaves a firm unable to pay.
input_signals.reasoning: The two best specifications in the archive each captured one half of this — the dual channel gave the strongest slope (-4.09) in ordinal form, and the cardinal single channel gave the strongest Sharpe and coverage — and because both deviations are expressed in the same units (weeks of sales) they can be added directly rather than rank-averaged, which removes the weighting ambiguity that the critic raised against nested rank composites. This is the most complete statement of the mechanism this search has identified.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( add( sub( ratio( invt, sale ), ma( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ), sub( ratio( sub( sub( act, che ), invt ), sale ), ma( ratio( sub( sub( act, che ), invt ), sale ), 5 ) ) ), 1 ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cardinal Overhang Against Uncovered Maturities
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dlc, che))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The relevant fragility is the fraction of near-term claims that cash cannot cover: a firm holding cash equal to its maturing debt faces no wall at all, while one holding almost none faces the whole of it, and that uncovered fraction is what turns excess inventory into a solvency problem.
input_signals.reasoning: Expressing coverage as dlc divided by dlc plus cash bounds the conditioner in the unit interval with a strictly non-negative denominator, which removes the near-zero and sign-flip pathologies the critic identified in the quick-asset denominator and guarantees the most constrained firms sit at the top of the rank rather than the bottom. It is also economically distinct from both archived conditioners: dlc/lt measures the composition of claims, while this measures the share of imminent claims with no cash behind them.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( sub( ratio( invt, sale ), ma( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ), 1 ), rank( ratio( dlc, add( dlc, che ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cardinal Overhang Against Timing And Cover
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), 1), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(ib, lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Two independent things must be true for an inventory overhang to become a solvency event: the debt must fall due soon, and the firm's earnings must be too small to service the liability stock; timing without a cash-flow problem is refinanceable, and weak earnings without near-term maturities buys years of time.
input_signals.reasoning: The three-way stack was redundant with an archived conjunction, so instead this replaces the structural-illiquidity leg with debt-service capacity — a flow measure of fragility that has never been paired with the overhang mechanism, and which is economically orthogonal to the timing of claims. Combining the two conditioners inside a single bounded rank keeps the signed cardinal leg in control of the sort direction while adding a genuinely new economic condition rather than a second encoding of illiquidity.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( sub( ratio( invt, sale ), ma( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ), 1 ), rank( sumrank( ratio( dlc, lt ), neg( ratio( ib, lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Lean Stock With Improving Quick Position
input_signals.hypothesis: Resilience shows as a firm running its stock at the low end of its own history while its cash and receivables strengthen relative to what it owes in the next year; the operating discipline and the improving payment capacity together mark a firm that will not be forced into a distressed adjustment.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than re-encoding the archived long-side signal, this changes both legs: the investment leg becomes a within-firm inventory *state* — the specification that beat flows repeatedly in this archive — and the conditioner becomes the improvement in the quick ratio, a payment-capacity trajectory never tested here and distinct from the maturity-mix change used before. Both legs are bounded ranks built from high-coverage annual items, so the long leg is populated by genuinely disciplined firms rather than by low-growth firms loading on CMA.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ts_rank( ratio( invt, sale ), 5 ) ) ), rank( delta( ratio( sub( act, invt ), lct ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Peer-Relative Stock Excess At The Maturity Wall
input_signals.hypothesis: The benchmark that matters competitively is what rivals carry, not what the firm itself used to carry: a firm holding materially more weeks of stock than its industry is losing the demand race, and if its debt is also short-dated it must discount that stock to raise cash.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the hyperparameter tweak with a different economic benchmark — peers rather than own history — which captures competitive mispositioning rather than internal drift and answers a question the archive has never posed for the flagship mechanism. Because industry adjustment requires no time-series history, the coverage gain comes from removing a five-year lookback requirement rather than from admitting sparse-history firms, and the cardinal encoding preserves the magnitude weighting that produced the best Sharpe in generation 8.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( ind_adj( ratio( invt, sale ) ), 1 ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )
